Harry Styles has said goodbye to New York the old-fashioned way: in print.

After 30 nights at Madison Square Garden, which wrapped on Halloween, he teamed up with The Village Voice for a free special-edition issue that includes a letter to the city. If you’re wondering what the Voice is, it was founded in Greenwich Village in 1955 by Dan Wolf, Ed Fancher and Norman Mailer, and it’s widely considered America’s first alternative newsweekly. For decades it covered the city’s arts, music and politics, and generations of New Yorkers found their first apartments in its classifieds, which may be the most New York legacy imaginable. It stopped printing in 2017, shut down in 2018, and returned in 2021.

Inside, Harry thanks New York for three months of welcome and says the dancing, the openness and the sheer joy of the crowds changed him. He signs off with “Until next time, take care of each other, New York.” Anna Wintour also contributes an op-ed with a very Anna take: Harry belongs on Broadway. There are features on his openers, including Tinashe, Jamie xx, Caroline Polachek and Lainey Wilson, plus spotlights on the charities the tour backed, from Planned Parenthood and Food Bank For NYC to HeadCount and Choose Love, and photos from across the run.

Copies were free, one per person, at 20+ spots around the city, from newsstands to record shops to a few 7-Elevens. Supplies were limited, so if you’re still hunting for one, good luck.

Since founding her eponymous label in 2020, @meryllrogge.personal has developed an eclectic approach to womenswear, interpreting the everyday wardrobe through an offbeat, playful lens. With previous stints at Marc Jacobs and Dries Van Noten, she is now balancing her own label with the role of creative director at Marni, a mantel she took up in 2025. Reading has become something of a luxury, reserved for “less chaotic times”.⁠
⁠
Her recent collaboration with @saintmartinbookshop offers a glimpse into that long-standing fascination. The project invites a rotating cast of friends of the house to curate capsule collections of one-of-a-kind books – independent publishing rarities of the kind Saint Martin has become synonymous with – set to accompany Rogge’s seasonal releases. For its first edition, ceramist and collaborator @elise_gettliffe, whose natural-glazed pottery explores the imperfections of traditional craft, takes the lead. ⁠
⁠
Across art, film and literature, Rogge finds herself drawn to the mundane – what she calls “the common thread”. “That’s why I like autobiographies. People who live extraordinary lives are always seen through the big picture, but I find comfort in their daily challenges.” This sensibility carries through to her selection for AnOther, a collection of books she describes as being as “fragmented as life itself”.⁠

The Paradox of the „Kaiser“: 
Re-evaluating Karl Lagerfeld’s Toughest Quotes

As we look at the visual history of high fashion, few figures loom larger than Karl Lagerfeld. He didn’t just design for houses like Chanel and Fendi; he fundamentally shaped the cultural dictionary of luxury for decades. However, part of the Lagerfeld brand was his unfiltered, highly provocative persona. His „Karlisms“—ranging from witty cultural commentary to deeply problematic statements on body image and societal norms, remain some of the most viral quotes in fashion history.
By looking at these quotes today, we are forced to confront a complex paradox. On one hand, Lagerfeld was a master of the fast-paced, ephemeral nature of style, once famously noting that „personality begins where comparison ends.“ On the other hand, his dogmatic stance on weight, including his infamous claim that „muscles are out, bones are in“ and his dismissive remarks regarding inclusivity reflect a bygone era of fashion gatekeeping.

In today’s landscape, where the industry increasingly champions body positivity, adaptive fashion, and genuine diversity, Lagerfeld’s most extreme statements serve as a stark reminder of the industry’s toxic past. Yet, separating the art from the artist remains a challenge. Lagerfeld’s work ethic was undeniable, but his rhetoric reminds us how much the conversation around empathy, respect, and inclusivity in fashion needed to evolve. 

Today, we can appreciate his monumental impact on design while simultaneously channeling that same fierce energy into building a more welcoming and conscious fashion community for the future.

For the Moschino Fall 2001 collection, the central idea was fashion as theatre. Under creative director Rossella Jardini, the runway became a playful portrayal of a woman’s everyday life, filled with exaggerated characters, domestic references and tongue-in-cheek stereotypes.
The show opened with a model wearing the now-famous “Maid in Italy” dress, carrying a bottle of wine. What followed was a parade of satin pyjamas, dressing gowns, hair curlers, cleaning uniforms and gingham dresses, before moving into businesswear, schoolboy-inspired looks and gangster references. Everyday roles were transformed into extravagant runway characters.
True to the house’s irreverent DNA, the collection blurred the line between fashion and costume, using humour and exaggeration to challenge conventional ideas of femininity. It was less about taking fashion seriously and more about having fun with it.

Bronze that looks like confectionery. A staircase made entirely of thread. A bench that trembles when someone approaches. At Art Mumbai 2026’s Sculpture Park, materials are doing things they were never expected to do.

But the transformations raise a more complicated question: what happens to a material’s history when it becomes art?
Before reaching a gallery, wood, metal, clay, and fibre have already lived other lives, shaped by landscapes, extraction, inherited knowledge, and generations of labour. In India, where the boundaries between art and craft have long been influenced by caste, class, and colonial ideas of value, those histories carry particular weight.

And while a sculpture may bear one artist’s name, its making can involve many more hands. Who gets recognised, what gets preserved, and which histories disappear when ordinary materials become extraordinary art?

John Frieda, the celebrity hairstylist who built a multimillion-dollar salon and commercial empire in the U.S. and U.K., has died following a long illness. He was 75.⁠
⁠
Frieda found fame at a young age, creating Joanna Lumley’s “Purdey” bowl cut in 1976 before opening high-end salons in London, New York City and Los Angeles. In 1989, he co-founded John Frieda Professional Hair Care with Gail Federici, building a business that was sold to Kao Corp. in 2002 for $450 million.⁠
⁠
The company’s first success was Frizz Ease, which launched in the U.K. before entering the U.S. mass market in 1990 and becoming a top-selling product worldwide. Sheer Blonde followed in 1998.⁠

Dr. Sarah Jukaku has found herself receiving more public attention following her husband Dr. Abdul El-Sayed's historic election to the United States Senate. Yet, Jukaku has built an accomplished career of her own as an Indian American psychiatrist based in Ann Arbor, Michigan.

Born and raised in Michigan to Indian immigrant parents, Jukaku's family traces their roots to Bhatkal, a coastal town in Karnataka, India. Her father studied medicine in Bengaluru before moving to the United States, where he established a career as a nephrologist.

Jukaku earned a bachelor's degree from University of Michigan and a master's degree from the University of Oxford. Jukaku then returned to the United States to study medicine at Columbia University's Vagelos College of Physicians and Surgeons, graduating in 2015. She completed her internship at Weill Cornell and NewYork-Presbyterian Hospital before returning to Michigan for her psychiatry residency at Michigan Medicine. She later served as co-chief of psychiatry at University Health Services and eventually founded her own Ann Arbor practice.

Her life has also been closely intertwined with the career of her husband who first attracted widespread national attention during his 2018 campaign for governor of Michigan. The two met while studying at the University of Michigan and married in 2006, while still undergraduates. They now live in Ann Arbor with their two daughters.

Last night's election marked a historic milestone for the family. El-Sayed's victory made him the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate, bringing national attention to his political career and renewed interest in the woman who has shared much of his journey.

But describing Jukaku simply as the wife of a historic political figure misses much of her story. She is an Indian American physician who pursued her education across some of the world's leading universities and medical institutions before returning to the state where she grew up to practise psychiatry and raise her family.
